reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Microphthalmia is an abnormally small, disorganised eye, whereas anophthalmia is the complete absence of ocular tissue; the two lie on a continuous spectrum
Both often coexist with coloboma as part of the microphthalmia-anophthalmia-coloboma (MAC) spectrum
Presentation ranges from an obviously small or absent eye to a clinically normal-looking eye with reduced axial length (nanophthalmos or posterior microphthalmos)
Frequently syndromic, with SOX2 and OTX2 among the most important causative genes, and association with chromosomal and multisystem disorders
Can be caused by genetic, chromosomal or environmental (including gestational infective and teratogenic) factors, so a broad aetiological workup is needed
True clinical anophthalmia is confirmed only when imaging shows no ocular tissue, as a rudimentary globe may be hidden
Early involvement of ocularists and orbital specialists supports socket and facial growth in severe cases
reference.pathophysiology: Microphthalmia and anophthalmia arise from disturbance of early eye morphogenesis. Normal eye formation depends on outgrowth of the optic vesicle from the developing forebrain and its invagination to form the optic cup, guided by a network of transcription factors including SOX2 and OTX2. Mutations in these developmental genes, chromosomal abnormalities, or environmental insults during embryogenesis can halt or distort this process, so the eye fails to grow to normal size (microphthalmia) or fails to develop at all (anophthalmia). Because the same signalling controls closure of the optic fissure, coloboma frequently coexists, and because these genes act in other tissues, associated brain, pituitary and systemic anomalies are common.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated coloboma at the milder end of the MAC spectrum
Cryptophthalmos and other eyelid or orbital malformations
Congenital cystic eye or orbital cyst
Phthisis bulbi from an acquired process mimicking a small eye
Nanophthalmos and posterior microphthalmos with a normal external appearance
Syndromic associations such as CHARGE syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Detailed ophthalmic examination and measurement of axial length by ocular biometry
Orbital and cranial imaging (ultrasound, CT or MRI) to confirm the presence and size of ocular tissue
Systemic and neurodevelopmental assessment, including for pituitary and brain anomalies
Chromosomal and molecular genetic testing including SOX2 and OTX2
Assessment of the fellow eye and orbit to guide prosthetic and reconstructive planning
redFlags: Bilateral severe microphthalmia or anophthalmia implying profound visual impairment
Associated neurological, endocrine or systemic anomalies requiring urgent evaluation
Progressive orbital or facial asymmetry from impaired socket growth
Family history indicating a heritable cause needing genetic counselling
reference.prognosis: Visual prognosis depends on the severity and laterality of the malformation, ranging from useful vision in mild unilateral microphthalmia to no vision in bilateral anophthalmia; in severe cases the focus shifts to promoting orbital and facial growth with expanders and prostheses, and overall outcome is strongly influenced by associated systemic conditions.
pitfalls: Diagnosing anophthalmia clinically without imaging to exclude hidden rudimentary ocular tissue
Overlooking associated brain, pituitary or systemic anomalies
Delaying socket expansion and prosthetic management, impairing orbital and facial development
Assuming a normal-appearing eye excludes posterior microphthalmos without biometry
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Promote orbital and mid-facial growth from infancy with progressively enlarging conformers, orbital expanders and ocular prostheses
Maximise and protect vision in any seeing eye with refractive correction, amblyopia therapy and protective eyewear
Manage coexisting ocular anomalies such as coloboma or cataract, and monitor for glaucoma and retinal detachment
Undertake systemic and neurodevelopmental assessment, including pituitary and brain evaluation, and treat any endocrine deficiency
Arrange molecular genetic testing (including SOX2 and OTX2) with genetic counselling and family assessment
Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary team of ophthalmology, oculoplastic surgery, clinical genetics and paediatrics
Provide low-vision rehabilitation and educational support
